title: The Oldest Song: Hurrian Hymn No. 6
summary: About 3,400 years ago, someone in the city of Ugarit (in modern Syria) pressed a hymn to the goddess Nikkal into clay, along with instructions for a singer and a nine-stringed lyre. Nobody agrees how to read the notation, so every reconstruction you hear today is a different guess.
thumbnailAlt: Thumbnail: a glowing clay tablet and an ancient lyre, titled The Oldest Song

title: The Dancing Plague of 1518
summary: In the summer of 1518, people in Strasbourg started dancing and couldn't stop. The city's "cure"? Hire musicians, build a stage, and keep them dancing. Historians still argue about why it happened.
thumbnailAlt: Thumbnail: a woodcut-style crowd dancing in a medieval Strasbourg street under the cathedral spire

title: Why Van Halen Banned Brown M&M's
summary: Van Halen's tour rider really did demand M&M's, with "absolutely no brown ones." David Lee Roth says it was a safety test hidden in the technical pages: if he found a brown M&M backstage, the promoter hadn't read the fine print, so the crew rechecked the whole stage. Skeptics say it was also great publicity.
thumbnailAlt: Thumbnail: bowls of colorful candy with the words No Brown M&M's, Why Van Halen really banned them

title: The 639-Year Concert
summary: An organ in a German church has been playing John Cage's "As Slow As Possible" since 2001, and it isn't due to finish until 2640. Sandbags hold the keys down, and the chord changes only on rare scheduled days, when crowds come to hear a pipe added or removed.
thumbnailAlt: Thumbnail for The 639-Year Concert: a church organ in Halberstadt playing As Slow As Possible

title: When Police Crashed the Beatles' Last Gig
summary: On January 30, 1969, the Beatles and Billy Preston played an unannounced set on the roof of their Apple building at 3 Savile Row in London while crowds gathered below. After complaints from local businesses the Metropolitan Police arrived, and after about 42 minutes John Lennon closed by saying he hoped they'd "passed the audition." It was the band's last public performance.
thumbnailAlt: Vintage-style view across city rooftops under a grey winter sky, titled The Beatles' Last Gig: The Rooftop Show Police Crashed

title: The Patron Tchaikovsky Never Met
summary: In late 1876 the wealthy Russian widow Nadezhda von Meck began writing to Tchaikovsky, and from 1877 she paid him an allowance of 6,000 rubles a year so he could compose full time, on one condition: they would never meet. For about 13 years they traded more than a thousand letters, and he dedicated his Fourth Symphony to her. In 1890 she suddenly ended the allowance, and historians still debate why.
thumbnailAlt: Vintage-style open wooden chest full of handwritten letters, titled The Patron He Never Met: 1,000+ letters, a pact never to meet

title: The Night Ozzy Bit a Bat
summary: On January 20, 1982, at Veterans Memorial Auditorium in Des Moines, Iowa, a fan threw a bat onto the stage during an Ozzy Osbourne concert. Ozzy said he thought it was a rubber toy when he put it in his mouth and bit its head off. After the show he got rabies shots at a local hospital, and the story followed him for the rest of his life.
thumbnailAlt: Vintage-style dark silhouette of a toy-like bat with spread wings on a concert stage, titled The Night Ozzy Bit a Bat: Des Moines, Iowa, January 1982

title: The Song They Called a Killer
summary: In 1933, Hungarian pianist Rezső Seress published the melody later known as "Gloomy Sunday." Newspapers and labels nicknamed it the suicide song, but the alleged links to suicides are largely unverified, and researchers found no clear causal connection.
thumbnailAlt: Vintage candlelit sheet music on a piano with rainy Budapest street mood through a window, no faces, titled The Song They Called a Killer
